title: This Is Flock’s AI Search Tool for Cops
gist: A WIRED code analysis of Flock Safety's AI-powered camera search tools -- including a natural-language 'FreeForm' person search and automated watch lists -- finds that content-moderation guardrails log and warn about misuse but do not actually block most abusive searches, arriving amid mounting police-misuse scandals, contract cancellations, and congressional scrutiny that pose real regulatory and reputational risk to Flock's business model.

insights.claim: Flock's software suite lets police search camera footage beyond license plates, including an AI-powered watch list where an officer cordons off a city area and cameras run a continuous automated search for anyone matching a written description, plus a natural-language 'FreeForm' search that converts both footage and typed descriptions into numerical embeddings for statistical ranking/matching.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: Flock has expanded well beyond its original license-plate-reader business into general-purpose AI person/vehicle search, materially broadening its product surface area (and associated legal/privacy risk) beyond its original core product category.

insights.claim: A 'People Detection Alert' feature requires no description at all: an officer draws a box within a single camera's field of view and is notified whenever a person enters it, triggered by as little as 75% model certainty that the object is a person.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: A 75%-confidence threshold for a location-based human-presence alert is a concrete, low reliability bar for a policing tool, quantifying the false-positive risk baked into the product.

insights.claim: Flock's content-moderation AI scores officer search descriptions against eight categories of sensitive content (including race, religion, nationality) and returns one of three verdicts -- allow, block, or warn -- based on a confidence score the department itself never sees; 'political, social, and cultural expression' is the only category that never blocks, only warns.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: Political/cultural expression -- the category with the strongest First Amendment protection -- is the one category Flock's system will never fully block, a design choice legal experts call backwards and a specific litigation/regulatory exposure point.

insights.claim: A warning (as opposed to a hard block) requires only that the officer tick an acknowledgment box and leave a comment before clicking 'Continue With Search Anyway' -- meaning warned searches are logged but not actually prevented.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: The core finding of the piece: Flock's celebrated safeguards function as an audit trail, not a control -- a material distinction for evaluating the company's public claims about protecting civil liberties versus the product's actual technical behavior.

insights.claim: Blocked categories (race, religion, nationality, offensive content) can reportedly be circumvented via workarounds -- e.g., the system blocks searches based on 'religion' but not on distinctive religious clothing, so an officer can search for a faith group's members by describing their dress instead.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: Demonstrated bypass methods for even the 'hard block' categories undermine Flock's core safety claims entirely, not just the warn-tier categories -- deepening the liability and reputational exposure beyond what the company's public messaging suggests.
insights.quote: Lots of people are having their images returned in response to these types of queries that would probably be upset if they knew about it.

insights.claim: In a real search example, an officer typed 'American flag': the search was blocked when aimed at finding a person, but the same term ran successfully across 11,000 cameras when aimed at finding vehicles instead -- illustrating an inconsistent double standard within the same moderation system.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: A concrete real-world example of the moderation system's inconsistency (11,000-camera search allowed via a mode-based loophole) is strong evidentiary ammunition for future litigation or regulatory action against Flock.

insights.claim: Departments can currently configure Flock's tools to allow searches without any reason or case number tied to a real investigation, and can leave off the automated system that flags suspicious use -- though Flock says these controls (case codes, shortened retention, automated auditing) will become mandatory by the end of the year.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: The gap between current (loose) and promised (year-end mandatory) safeguards represents both near-term legal exposure and a concrete compliance-deadline catalyst to track for whether Flock actually follows through.

insights.claim: Audit Assistance, a feature Flock announced this spring to surface misuse patterns, is off by default in the code WIRED reviewed, though Flock says more than a third of its customers had enabled it as of August.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: A default-off safety feature with roughly one-third opt-in adoption after months of availability suggests weak organic uptake of self-policing tools absent a hard mandate, a relevant KPI for evaluating whether Flock's voluntary reforms will meaningfully reduce misuse before regulation forces the issue.

insights.claim: When a South Carolina sheriff's office turned on Audit Assistance, an internal-affairs officer identified more than 2,700 allegedly unauthorized searches the very next day.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: A single-department, single-day discovery of 2,700 flagged searches is a striking scale indicator of latent misuse across Flock's customer base -- implying the true scope of abuse industry-wide, once more agencies enable auditing, could be a significant emerging liability and PR risk for the company.

insights.claim: Data on flagged/warned searches flows back to Flock itself -- the officer's language, the assigned category and confidence score, and what the officer did next (continue, dismiss, dispute) -- but Flock's statement to WIRED did not address how long these records are retained, who inside the company can access them, or whether they're used to evaluate/improve the moderation system.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: Flock's non-disclosure on data retention/access practices for sensitive flagged-search data is a governance transparency gap that regulators or plaintiffs' attorneys could target in future scrutiny.

themes.theme: Documented officer misuse and regulatory backlash

insights.claim: At least 50 US officers have recently been charged with or accused of misusing license plate readers according to the Washington Post, with 46 of those cases involving Flock specifically; in more than half, the target was a current or former romantic partner or their new partner.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: Flock accounts for the overwhelming majority (46 of 50) of documented recent license-plate-reader misuse cases nationally, a specific, quantified liability data point directly implicating the company's product design and oversight, not just generic industry risk.

insights.claim: Documented individual misuse cases include a Milwaukee officer who searched a woman he was dating 124 times (logging each as an 'investigation'), a Georgia police chief who ran his ex-girlfriend and her daughter 600 times before being charged and later taking his own life, and a Kansas chief who ran his ex 164 times and lost his badge without being charged.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: These extreme, repeated-abuse case studies (100+ searches per victim) demonstrate the system's audit logging alone did not prevent sustained stalking behavior, reinforcing the piece's core finding that logging is not deterrence.

insights.claim: Over the past year Flock has faced a wave of business-level backlash: police departments canceling contracts, city councils reversing prior approvals, two members of Congress writing to CEO Garrett Langley after a Texas deputy searched over 83,000 cameras for a woman who had an abortion, and Illinois finding Flock let federal immigration agents access state camera data in violation of state law.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: Direct, quantifiable revenue and regulatory risk: contract cancellations, congressional scrutiny, and a state-law compliance violation (Illinois/ICE data sharing) represent concrete near-term threats to Flock's government-contract revenue base and expansion trajectory.

insights.claim: An 83,000-camera search was reportedly run by a single Texas deputy searching for a woman who had an abortion -- an extreme-scale example that directly prompted congressional letters to Flock's CEO.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: This single incident is Flock's most reputationally damaging documented case and a proximate trigger for federal political attention -- a named, high-visibility risk event relevant to assessing regulatory momentum against the company.

themes.theme: Expert framing: structural surveillance risk beyond individual misuse

insights.claim: ACLU policy analyst Jay Stanley describes Flock's moderation system as 'a speck on the back of a giant surveillance machine' that can be probed by AI for 'your-imagination-is-the-limit fishing expeditions,' arguing the company's recent reforms target only 'bad-apple cops' while leaving the structural mass-surveillance risk of the underlying database untouched.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: The ACLU's framing reorients the risk from individual-officer scandal (addressable via PR/product patches) to the systemic existence of a searchable historical camera database itself -- a much harder, existential regulatory risk (e.g. outright bans, moratoria) that individual guardrail fixes cannot resolve.
insights.quote: a speck on the back of a giant surveillance machine

insights.claim: UC San Diego trust-and-safety researcher Deepak Kumar notes that warnings deter only officers not already determined to misuse a system, drawing on parallel research in online-harassment interfaces where motivated users sometimes did more harm after being warned, and stresses that effective moderation requires scrutinizing both search inputs AND outputs, not just inputs.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: Kumar's input-only-moderation critique is a specific, actionable product gap: Flock's system only screens what officers type in, never what the AI returns, a known best-practice failure mode from broader AI safety research applicable to any AI-search vendor being evaluated for governance robustness.
insights.quote: Best practice examines both inputs and outputs, which is why so many AI safety efforts now check both to prevent models from generating harmful outputs.

insights.claim: Governance responsibility is largely delegated to local police agencies rather than centralized by Flock: a former police chief (Don De Lucca) confirms vendors can only recommend safeguards, while departments must set their own access rules, with search reach determined by search mode, agency permissions, and inter-agency data-sharing agreements (including statewide/nationwide networks for some plate searches).
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: A fragmented, thousands-of-agencies governance model means Flock's actual misuse-prevention efficacy varies enormously by local department policy, making company-wide risk difficult to underwrite or regulate uniformly -- a structural governance risk for both investors and policymakers.
